title: Hurricane Nolo Is Crawling Toward Hawaii — And It's Carrying a Lot of Rain
summary:
Imagine a storm that moves slower than you walk. That's Hurricane Nolo. On Friday it was spinning toward Hawaii at only 5 miles per hour — about the speed of a slow bike ride.

People on the Big Island are under a hurricane watch. That means hurricane weather could arrive in 24 to 36 hours. Nolo probably won't crash into land. But it has two scary tricks: it's slow, and it's soaking wet.

Forecasters say some places could get more than 2 feet of rain. Most areas will see 10 to 25 inches. The National Hurricane Center warned about "life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides."

Right now Nolo's winds are 105 mph — a Category 2 storm. Over the next three days they could grow to 140 mph. That would make it a Category 4, a major hurricane.

Hawaii has already had a rough year. Four big disasters have damaged or destroyed about 1,290 homes. Governor Josh Green says recovery could cost around $1 billion.

Nolo's path has been weird, too. Earlier this week it suddenly turned right and headed straight for the Big Island. Last week, forecasters even thought it was falling apart. Then it came back to life.

Hurricane season in Hawaii lasts until November 30. So keep an eye on the Pacific!
why_it_matters: Learning how storms are tracked and how a hurricane watch works helps families get ready in time — the same way your school practices a safety drill before anything happens.

background_read: Hawaii is a group of islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, thousands of miles away from the U.S. mainland.
Hurricanes need warm ocean water to grow, and the water near Hawaii is usually cooler, so big storms often weaken before they reach the islands.
Even so, Hawaii has been hit before — in 1992 Hurricane Iniki struck the island of Kauai and caused serious damage.
Article_Structure: WHO: Hurricane Nolo, forecasters at the National Hurricane Center, and Hawaii's Governor Josh Green.
WHAT: A slow-moving hurricane is headed toward Hawaii, bringing more than 2 feet of rain and the chance it grows into a Category 4 storm.
WHERE: The Big Island of Hawaii, in the middle of the Pacific Ocean.
WHY: The storm moves very slowly and carries huge amounts of rain, so the danger is life-threatening flooding and mudslides — and Hawaii is already recovering from four disasters this year.

perspectives.perspective: Hawaii residents on the Big Island
perspectives.description: They are hurrying to prepare for days of heavy rain and are worried about floods and mudslides near their homes.
They warn people early and say the slow, soaking storm is dangerous even if it never actually crashes into land.

perspectives.perspective: People watching the storm from a distance
perspectives.description: They feel a little relieved that Nolo may stay offshore, but they know the rain alone could still cause serious damage to homes and roads.
